To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have developed a tool which takes a description of an access control system in a simple but expressive language and generates a verified XACML policy script.

we have developed an algorithm to translate the access control system descriptions to XACML scripts, and we have implemented a prototype tool that can generate XACML scripts based on the access control system specifications.
the tool can be used for generating XACML scripts that implement access control systems that can be verified to satisfy policies, and that the tool is available for public use.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (i) Can we generate XACML scripts that can be verified to be implementing a given policy? (ii) How do we verify that a given policy is satisfied by a given system?

the development of a tool for the generation of XAML scripts from access control specifications, and the formal verification of such specifications against the policies they are supposed to implement.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have developed a tool which generates XACML scripts, which implement the policies of a given system and can be verified using a tool such as the X-Access tool [2] to be implementing these policies.
our tool allows us to generate XACML scripts that can be verified by a theorem prover.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of XACML is not limited to the analysis of access control systems, but it is also a useful tool in the construction of such systems.

the use of a formal language for describing access control systems and policies, and the use of automated tools for generating the corresponding XACML code, allows for the generation of XAML scripts for which we can be confident that they correctly implement the desired policies.

we have shown that the verification of access control policies is not limited to the systems that can be described in the simple language we have used, but can be applied to systems described using a standard language such as XACML.
